But is it really the case that some of us look back with
gratitude and joy and others with disillusionment and
doubt? Is it not rather true that all of us to some extent share
in both these moods? Which of us could justifiably complain
that the term has not brought him some degree of good,
summoning him to give thanks? And who would not have
to confess that neither is he at the goal of his hopes and aims,
that not all of his desires and hopes have found fulfilment?
Who must not confess that he himself has been found wanting
at many points, again and again?
We ought all to realize that in whatever the term has
brought us, both of joy and bitter sorrow, the pressure of
Christ has been upon us to free us from the fetters of our-
selves, to bring us the freedom of the spirit in which to meet
the challenge of the future. And if we have not yet become
conscious of this, then this hour of worship at the end of term
should bring it home to us, this hour in which the word of
Scripture meets and finds us, compelling us to understand
our lives in its light, permitting us to understand our lives
in its light.
Free to meet the challenge of the future! Are we sure of the
future? Are we sure of ourselves in regard to the future?
"Brethren, I do not consider that I have made it my own."
The lives of us all are governed by this motif of the "not yet".
The goal still lies before us and we are not yet what we shall
be. "But one thing I do, forgetting what lies behind and
straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on to the prize
of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus."
Intertwined with the motif of the "not yet" runs that of the
"no longer", and the "no longer"—i.e. our emancipation
from the old Adam—enables us bravely to bear the "not
yet" and to run the race towards the goal that beckons us.
